name: Kojic acid

lead: Kojic acid is a compound made by Aspergillus fungi, including in rice fermented for sake, and is used in brightening creams, serums and soaps to lighten dark spots, acne marks and melasma.

It binds copper at the active site of tyrosinase, blocking the enzyme that begins melanin production, and it has antioxidant activity. Reviews list it among conventional first-line topical agents for hyperpigmentation. In a 60-patient Indian study, 4 percent hydroquinone acted faster than a 0.75 percent kojic acid cream that also contained vitamin C, and other trials test it inside combination products.

paras: People use it as a cream, serum or soap, often as part of a brightening routine with sunscreen and other pigment-fading ingredients. Results typically build over weeks to months. It is sensitive to light and air, so packaging matters.

Contact dermatitis and irritation are the main concerns. In the EU a 2024 regulation allows it only in face and hand products at up to 1 percent, applying to products placed on the market from 1 November 2025. Long-term safety data are limited, and it does not replace sun protection.

angle.text: Kojic acid is used in brightening creams and soaps to lighten dark spots, acne marks and melasma. It blocks the pigment-making enzyme, so patches fade gradually. Small studies have looked at melasma; irritation is commonly reported, and under-eye use has been studied less.

lead: Kojic acid is an organic compound, a derivative of 4-pyrone, produced by several fungi, notably Aspergillus oryzae (known in Japan as koji), and formed as a by-product when rice is fermented for sake.[1] It chelates metal ions, including copper and iron, and is used in food to prevent browning and in cosmetics to lighten skin.[1][2]

In skin care it appears in soaps, creams and serums for melasma, dark spots and uneven tone. It inhibits tyrosinase, the copper-containing enzyme that begins melanin synthesis, and reviews list it among conventional first-line topical agents for hyperpigmentation alongside hydroquinone and glycolic acid.[2][3][4]

Trial evidence is moderate to limited. A 60-patient Indian study found 4 percent hydroquinone acted faster than a 0.75 percent kojic acid cream that also contained vitamin C,[5] and other trials have tested kojic acid in combination products.[6] In the European Union its cosmetic use is restricted: a 2024 regulation allows it only in face and hand products at up to 1 percent, applying to products placed on the market from 1 November 2025.[1]
infobox: Aspergillus fungi (koji); fermentation of rice and carbohydrates

Sold as a cosmetic ingredient; restricted in the EU

paras: Kojic acid is used to lighten melasma and other pigmentation and appears in cleansers, soaps, creams and serums, sometimes with turmeric extracts or vitamin C.[1][5][7] A US over-the-counter listing for a turmeric kojic acid facial cleanser describes its use as cleansing facial skin only.[7]

Kojic acid is used on cut fruit to limit browning, in seafood to preserve color, as an antibacterial and antifungal agent, and as a precursor to the flavorant maltol.[1] Reviews describe pharmaceutical research on derivatives with antimicrobial, antioxidant and other properties.[2]

Reviews of melasma treatment describe hydroquinone and triple combination creams as the best-studied topical agents, with kojic acid among alternatives and combination partners.[3][4][8] A 2013 prospective study in 60 patients with facial melasma compared nightly 4 percent hydroquinone with 0.75 percent kojic acid plus 2.5 percent vitamin C: kojic acid showed no significant MASI change at week 4 and significant decreases at weeks 8 and 12, while hydroquinone improved significantly from week 4, and the authors reported hydroquinone as superior at each time point.[5] The study had no placebo control and a short 12-week follow-up, and vitamin C in the kojic acid arm limits attribution.[5]

A 2025 split-face pilot tested a cosmetic with 5 percent alpha-arbutin and 2 percent kojic acid against triple combination cream, and other studies tested kojic acid inside combination products. Research with human tyrosinase has noted that many inhibitors identified with mushroom tyrosinase lack clinical efficacy.[9]

Human studies include the 60-patient comparison with hydroquinone,[5] a randomized comparison of treatments in solar lentigines of Asian women,[10] a study of actinic lentigines under bleaching treatment,[11] comparisons of melasma modalities and chemical peels,[12][13] and a split-face pilot with alpha-arbutin plus kojic acid. Reviews and consensus include a 2026 Pigmentary Disorders Society Delphi consensus with 38 dermatologists,[14] and reviews of topical melasma therapy, multimodal management and kojic acid applications.[2][3][4][8]
A registered trial of a peeling product for melasma (n=10) and trials of herbal creams and adjuvant programs are listed.[15][16][17]

Reviews describe contact dermatitis and irritation as the main concerns and note that kojic acid is unstable in light and air.[2] Wikipedia states that kojic acid may be weakly carcinogenic according to some animal studies, is not believed to reach carcinogenic thresholds in human skin and is considered safe at cosmetic levels, while the EU has restricted its cosmetic concentration to 1 percent in face and hand products.[1] In the hydroquinone comparison, mild erythema or burning was reported in a small number of patients in each arm, although the paper's results and discussion differ on the figures.[5]

Kojic acid inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme that starts melanin synthesis, and chelates copper at its active site; it also has antioxidant activity.[2] Kojate, the deprotonated form, binds ferric iron to give a red complex, which may reflect its biological role in solubilizing iron.[1]

The compound has the formula HOCH2C5H2O2OH (5-hydroxy-2-hydroxymethyl-4H-pyran-4-one). Labelling studies indicate at least two biosynthetic routes, mainly via dehydration of glucose; industrial production relies on aerobic fermentation.[1]

Grokipedia, an AI-generated source treated with caution, states it was isolated in 1907 by Kendo Saito from Aspergillus oryzae and named by Teijiro Yabuta in 1912.[18] A 1956 chemistry review covers early work on the compound.[19] The 2024 EU regulation limiting its cosmetic use is the most recent regulatory step in the sources reviewed.[1]
The forum sources reviewed contain no substantive discussion of kojic acid.

timeline.event: Kojic acid reportedly isolated from Aspergillus oryzae by Kendo Saito (per Grokipedia).[18]
